name: HC-SR04 Ultrasonic Rangefinder
summary: Ping-and-listen distance sensor, 2 cm to 4 m. Four pins, 5 V only, and an echo pin that will happily feed 5 V into a 3.3 V board.
notes: ECHO drives a 5 V pulse. Into an ESP32, a Pico or any 3.3 V board that needs a divider, two resistors is enough. This is the most common way the sensor kills a GPIO.
Trigger with a 10 us high pulse, then time how long ECHO stays high. Distance in cm is that time in microseconds divided by 58, because sound makes the round trip twice.
Below about 2 cm it cannot distinguish the echo from its own transmit burst, so it returns nonsense rather than a small number. Treat anything under the blind zone as invalid.
It needs a reasonably flat target square to the sensor. Soft, angled or narrow objects scatter the ping and read as out of range.
If ECHO never goes low because nothing came back, a naive pulseIn blocks. Always use a timeout.
The HC-SR04P and the RCWL-1601 are pin-compatible and run from 3 to 5.5 V, which removes the level shifting problem entirely. Worth buying instead.
Readings drift with temperature: the speed of sound changes about 0.17 percent per degree C. Over a 30 degree swing that is a few centimetres at 4 m.

pins.name: VCC
pins.note: 5 V. The sensor draws a 15 mA burst on each ping.

pins.name: TRIG
pins.note: 10 us high pulse starts a measurement.

pins.name: ECHO
pins.note: Outputs 5 V. Divide it down for a 3.3 V board.

circuit.title: Level shifting the echo

parts.why: In series with the 5 V echo output, the top half of a divider into a 3.3 V input.
The lower half. 5 V across 1k and 2k puts 3.3 V on the junction, which is what the input sees.
Across the supply at the module. Each ping pulls a 15 mA burst and a long thin lead sags under it.

circuit.note: TRIG is an input and tolerates a 3.3 V drive, so only ECHO needs the divider. The module has no 3.3 V variant worth trusting: the ones sold as 3 V parts are usually the same board with a different regulator.
